cvEn:
Dvir Zion Revah, son of Ashira and Avraham, was born on 25 Heshvan 5757 (7 November 1996) in Jerusalem. He was the eldest brother of Tamir, Mor and Ido.
He was the husband of Or and the father of Tzur and Par.

Dvir grew up and was educated in the Pisgat Ze'ev neighborhood of Jerusalem. He was a charming, gentle child, a good boy who loved to play basketball and spend time with his family and friends.

He studied at the Hanan Torah elementary school and continued to the Kiryat Noar religious high school. In ninth grade he studied at Hasmonaim, and in tenth grade he transferred to the ORT Gva'at Ram college, where he completed his studies. Dvir was a mischievous and stubborn youth who wanted to do everything his own way. He was occasionally absent from school and did not put much effort into his studies; he spent many hours with his friends, who were at the center of his world.

Dvir loved music. He learned to play the drums, taught himself the piano, completed a professional DJ course, and created electronic music together with his brother Tamir.

When the time came to sit for his matriculation exams, Dvir's parents promised him a car if he passed his final exams with full success. Dvir took this seriously: after each exam he came home and told his parents, "Here's the steering wheel, here are the windows..." In the end, his determination brought him what he wanted.

In eleventh grade, Dvir and his classmates traveled to Poland. Dvir saw the trip as deeply meaningful, because of his special bond with his grandfather, a Holocaust survivor. From the day Dvir was born, his connection with Grandpa Yaakov was special. Dvir wanted to know everything about his grandfather's past and to learn from all his deeds. His grandfather, for his part, did not like to talk about the past, and Dvir's wish to know brought them closer. The bond was deep and influenced Dvir greatly. Dvir was always ready to help his grandparents with anything, whenever they called him and even when they did not. Before the trip to Poland, Dvir insisted on going to his grandfather's orphanage in Poland. This was not part of the planned route, but Dvir did not give up. Even when he was permitted to go there, it was not simple: the place had changed, and Dvir had to bring maps and photographs and, with great determination, finally reached the exact location. While he was there he photographed the site for his grandfather, who was deeply moved. From then on, they always told each other that they would travel to Poland together to make this roots journey, something they had not managed to do. The visit to the orphanage affected Dvir profoundly and strengthened his desire to serve in a meaningful role in the army, in order to make an impact and create change.

At ORT high school, Dvir was directed to the technician-and-matriculation track (TAV), and as part of it he studied in the thirteenth and fourteenth grades. Toward the end of the track, Dvir decided he wanted to be a combat soldier. He understood that if he completed his studies with army funding, he would be assigned to the Air Force and could not serve in a combat role. He therefore gave up the funding, against his parents' wishes, and paid for his years of study himself, so that he could go through the screening for the combat roles he wanted.

As he was finishing his studies and preparing to enter military service, Dvir felt a desire to study more and strengthen his religious path. In his free time he attended Torah classes, grew stronger in faith, and consolidated his path, drawing closer to his rabbi, Rabbi Yaakov Shimon, who had guided him since his youth.

On 22 July 2015 he enlisted in the IDF and served as a combat soldier in the 932nd Battalion of the Nahal Brigade. After basic training he went on to the commanders' course for squad leaders, and later continued to the officers' course. During one of the navigation exercises in the course, Dvir was injured in his hand. He continued the navigation despite the injury and made no fuss about it. When the exercise ended and his commander learned of his condition, he ordered Dvir to go to the hospital to treat his hand. Dvir underwent surgery, and his hand needed time to heal. At the same time, the course included a "Lauren test," which Dvir had to pass. He took the test with his injury, and because of it he could not climb the rope that was part of the exam. As a result, he faced the danger of being dismissed from the course, but he insisted on staying. He brought his request to the brigade commander, who gave him another opportunity to complete the part he had missed. Dvir took the test with his hand still injured, proved that his performance had not been impaired, and successfully completed the course.

Because of the injury, he was assigned to the role of security officer at a classified facility. Once he recovered, he became a platoon commander in the Palhod (the vanguard company), which Dvir loved. He was devoted to his soldiers and to the military profession, and he finished as an outstanding platoon commander. He then served as deputy commander of the vanguard company. Dvir valued the human connection with his soldiers; in the role of deputy company commander the connection is less personal and more of an executive arm of the company commander, but Dvir continued his way of forging a close-knit group out of the members of his unit, and he was loved by all his soldiers.

As part of his preparation for the role of company commander, Dvir was selected for the MALTAK program, in which he completed a degree in political science combined with military and security studies. Dvir knew that after MALTAK he would serve as a company commander in the Training Base of the Nahal Brigade, and during his degree he was occupied with thoughts and actions that would guide him to become a meaningful commander. He met special people from whom he believed he could learn, and he did everything to become the best commander when he finished his studies.

At the beginning of the MALTAK period, Dvir married Or. The two loved each other with a deep and intense love. After their wedding they lived together in Sha'arei Tikva and had a son, Tzur. Dvir's family was the center of his world. As a career soldier he had to learn to balance home and the army, and with all the constraints and demands, Dvir always gave his wife and son the best experiences, and the time he spent with them was always devoted and meaningful, even when it was short.

After completing MALTAK, he served as company commander in the Nahal Brigade's Training Base. At the end of that role he returned to the battalion and served as the battalion's operations officer, and at the beginning of this role he was in Hebron until the war broke out.

On Shabbat, 22 Tishrei, Simchat Torah 5784, 7 October 2023, at 6:30 in the morning, the Hamas terror organization launched a surprise attack on Israel. Under cover of massive rocket and missile fire from the Gaza Strip on wide areas of the country, thousands of terrorists infiltrated by land, sea and air and launched a murderous assault on the communities of the Gaza envelope, on Sderot, Ofakim and Netivot, on a music festival near the kibbutzim Re'im and Nir Oz, on IDF bases, and on travelers on the roads in the area. The terrorists murdered some eight hundred civilians in their homes and in their cars, after committing grave crimes against them. They abducted hundreds of Israelis into the Gaza Strip and destroyed, looted and set fire to homes and property. Hundreds of soldiers, police officers, security personnel and members of the local emergency squads fell in battle. That morning, a war began.

Dvir took an active part in the fighting from its first day, first as operations officer in the 932nd Battalion of the Nahal Brigade, and later was appointed commander of the battalion's Palhod (vanguard company) and was slated to become deputy battalion commander. For many months he fought in the Gaza Strip and led his company in a series of complex and daring operations, including the operation to take control of Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, in which his soldiers captured hundreds of terrorists.

Because of the fighting, Dvir suffered a severe herniated disc in his back, but he continued to command his company naturally, with devotion and composure. The personal pain he carried did not diminish his professionalism; Dvir made every effort to keep running forward and leading. In Dvir's value system, being at the front, leading his soldiers and protecting their lives during combat was more important than preserving his own health and comfort.

Throughout the fighting, Dvir knew how to inspire his soldiers to follow him, to strengthen them and his fellow commanders in difficult moments, and to push everyone around him to perform better.

During the war, Dvir and Or announced to the family that they were expecting a daughter.

In October 2024, Major Netanel Hershkovitz, the husband of Dvir's cousin, fell in battle. The tragedy deeply shook the family, and Dvir in particular, who had a special bond with Netanel.

Three months later, on Monday, 6 Tevet 5785, 6 January 2025, while Dvir was commanding his company on an operational activity in Beit Hanoun in the northern Gaza Strip, an explosive device was detonated against the force. Dvir was killed on the spot. His deputy, Captain Eitan Israel Shechnie, was killed with him.

Major Dvir Zion Revah fell in battle on 6 Tevet 5785 (6 January 2025). He was twenty-eight years old. He was laid to rest in the Military Cemetery on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem. He left behind a pregnant wife and a son, his parents, a sister and two brothers.

A few months after his death, his wife Or gave birth to their daughter, Par.

Dvir, his family wrote, was a value-driven, creative, responsible and professional commander, with strategic thinking and the ability to see moves ahead. As in his personal life, in the army he always sought to improve what existed and to do good. He was a personal example, he spread a sense of security around him, and he always knew how to find a proper solution to every problem.

He was attentive to his soldiers and cared for them as if they were his own children, but he also set high demands for them and maintained an uncompromising professional standard. Dvir insisted on procedures with his soldiers and saw this as protecting their lives. Even when they were outside of combat, he instilled in them the discipline of following procedures, because he saw it as a way to protect his soldiers from harm.

"I cannot count how many times my life or the lives of other soldiers were saved thanks to him, thanks to the discipline he instilled in us," one of his soldiers said. "Even if it meant being a little tough on us, even if it meant sitting his soldiers down to go through event debriefings with them and teaching them how to deal with combat situations. He said to us: 'I don't need the soldiers to like me, I need them to come back safely to their mothers.'"

Modesty and humility were rooted in Dvir's character. With his flexibility he knew how to be a bold and leading commander while keeping his gentleness. In every role he filled he excelled and was praised, but he never sought to stand out. He acted with devotion, modesty and humility, out of genuine love for the people of Israel and the land of Israel.

His wife Or says that from the day they met, Dvir prepared her for the possibility of war, telling her that when it happened, they would not see each other for a long time, because he would devote himself entirely to the success of the mission and would not leave the battlefield.

"A dear man, so beloved to me," Or eulogized. "I carry you with me as part of my soul into the world. From the first moment I met you I knew you were mine. You have a magic over me that always brought life into me. I always loved following you and being with you; every piece of advice or choice you made brought me happiness. Thank you for who you are to me, for the spirit you breathe into me...

Other people's words or actions never managed to divert you from what truly matters to you, and you never felt ashamed or afraid to bring your truth into the world... You are a firm, steady rock, full of strength, a strength that also includes silence and humility. You never wanted to tell or to glorify your name, and you never acted for that. Truth, your deep roots and the good of the collective were always before your eyes. From that place you always strove for professionalism, and you did everything in the best possible way."

"Last night I went through all our messages from the past year," wrote Tamir, a fellow soldier, "and in all of them there was a recurring theme: faith. You simply enjoy and believe in what you do. You enjoy fighting, commanding, defending the country, you enjoy the meaning. You are the rare kind who truly, sincerely believes that our role in the world is to do good for another person, for our people... I have never seen devotion like yours. There was a lot of courage in you, a lot of strength, and so much determination... You brought a spirit of victory, of friendship, of devotion and faith without end."

The battalion commander related that Dvir was the only one in the entire battalion who fought alongside him throughout the war, almost without going home, and that even when he suffered a severe herniated disc, he insisted on continuing to fight. The battalion commander further said: "When you took over as company commander, you immediately brought new things from yourself. In our clashes you were always first, pushing for contact, moving forward. Throughout that period you never did anything for yourself; you never wanted to be in the spotlight, only hard work, with everything in your hands. Even great successes you never credited to yourself; it was always the one under you or beside you."

After Dvir's death, a prayer he had written during his service was published: "May it be Your will, Lord my God and God of my fathers, that You send a blessing upon my deeds, and grant me the ability to sanctify Your name in the world, and to succeed in my deeds in guarding Your holy state, and to learn how to win the wars of duty that threaten Your holy people. Please, my God, make me a vessel for Your mission. Help me sanctify Your name in the world."

A memorial page for Dvir was opened on Instagram, under the name remember_dvir_revah.
